task: verify a claim, image, or story online: take a specific claim or viral post and check it — search what fact-checkers say (Snopes, PolitiFact, AP/Reuters fact check), trace the original source and its date/context (lateral reading), and/or reverse-image-search a photo to find its true origin; complete when a supported verdict (true/false/miscaptioned/unproven) is reached with the checked sources on screen. Surface pinned: a live verification session on real claims — media-literacy lectures without a worked example are off-task.

tree.label: Fact-check a viral claim
tree.note: 1 runs in every keeper. 2 runs where a fact-checker is asked directly, and fU9D and F6MD go there first and stop there. 3 runs in the ten keepers with an image or a frame, and 3.7 runs the search again. 4 follows every search that finds a page. 5 runs where the user has to judge the source itself - t8lK stays on 5 throughout, and linG runs it on an official account. 6 runs in 4Rh4, 6KeC and VOgi, where the search only dated the footage and the place still has to be found. 7 runs in VxnK and VOgi, where the claim is checked against a reference. 8 closes every run, and 8.7 loops back to 1 for the next claim in qW96, 6KeC, q5N5 and fU9D.

children.label: Pin the claim
children.note: 1.1 in every keeper. 1.2 in the three keepers that look at who posted it and how far it went. 1.3 where the image or the post itself shows a time, a place or profile details. 1.4 where the image or the chat is read for plausibility before any tool is opened. 1.5 in every keeper, where the user decides what goes into the tool, and F6MD runs it twice because the first phrase found nothing.

questions.question: Which of these posts is the claim you want checked?
questions.why: The screen shows a tweet by [name] about atrocities in Bengal, establishing the specific viral claim that will anchor the verification process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means you lose the opportunity to select a viral claim that is personally relevant or currently prevalent in your own social media feed.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked one post to check first - check it is the claim you sent it and not another post on the same feed; the feed showed several.
questions.check: Does the page show more than one distinct post or claim that the person could mean?
questions.say_example: Found more than one post about <the flood>. I'll check <the one about the bridge collapse>. OK, or a different one?

questions.question: What exactly does the post or its comments claim?
questions.why: Pausing to read the comments by [name] and [name] establishes the exact details about the moon's rotation and location-based appearance that need to be verified.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally read the exact phrasing of the original claims, which helps in understanding the specific nuances to investigate.
questions.check: What does the post or its comments state as the claim, in their own words?
questions.say_example: The post claims <the moon looks the same from every city>. That's what I'm checking.

questions.question: Does the post carry a warning label or Community Note?
questions.why: Social media platforms often append visual warning labels or community-contributed context directly below viral misinformation, providing an immediate flag that the claim is disputed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the time-saving benefit of noticing an existing platform-level debunk if the agent only reads the user-generated text and misses the visually distinct warning label.
questions.check: Does the post display a platform warning label or Community Note beneath it?
questions.say_example: This post has a Community Note under it. It says <the photo is from 2016>.

questions.question: Did the search stay on your claim, or drift to another one in the results?
questions.why: The search results show an unrelated claim about PETA and Major League Baseball alongside the Biden quotes, offering a chance to explore a different viral topic.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the freedom to browse the peripheral search results and spontaneously pivot to a different viral claim that catches your interest.
questions.verify_form: The agent stayed on your claim or wandered to another one in the results - check it stayed.
questions.check: Did the search open a different claim from the results instead of staying on the one it was given?
questions.say_example: The results also show <a different claim, about a stadium>. I'm staying on yours.

questions.question: Do the copies in the results add anything, or just repeat the post's caption?
questions.why: Examining the grid of YouTube and Instagram results reveals the specific false captions and the viral scale of the claim before you begin debunking it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the firsthand visual context of exactly how the misinformation was framed and distributed across different social media platforms.
questions.verify_form: The agent looked at how far the claim spread, or skipped that - check whether it noted the captions the copies carry; the copies repeat the claim, they do not answer it.
questions.check: Do the grid of copies/results found for this post simply repeat the same caption as the original claim, without adding new information?
questions.say_example: These <12> results all carry the same caption as the post. They're copies, so they don't settle anything.

questions.question: What source video is being analyzed here?
questions.why: The narrator explicitly names the Nibiru Channel video on screen and sarcastically notes the creator's financial motive for generating clicks, which establishes the exact claim being investigated.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose direct exposure to the narrator's sarcastic tone and the critical context regarding the original creator's click-driven financial motivations.
questions.check: Does the page name a specific video/channel being analyzed (title, uploader)?
questions.say_example: Found the source video - <'Strange light over the bay'>, from <a channel with 40k subscribers>

questions.question: Does the name of the page that shared this suggest satire or novelty rather than news?
questions.why: The image is posted by 'Weird Tales Magazine', which immediately signals that the content is curated for bizarre or sensational oddities rather than factual news.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate contextual clue provided by the publisher's name, which helps set the appropriate level of skepticism before starting the verification.
questions.check: What is the name of the account or page that shared this post, and does that name suggest a satire, meme, or novelty source rather than news?
questions.say_example: This was shared by <a page that posts odd stories>. It isn't a news outlet.

questions.question: Were the account's other posts looked at, not just its follower count?
questions.why: Although the profile shows a massive following of over 277,000 users, checking their timeline would reveal if the account operates as a dedicated misinformation node.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the contextual understanding of whether this highly followed account has a history of spreading similar false claims.
questions.verify_form: The agent may have skipped the poster's timeline - check whether it looked at the account's other posts; the follower count alone says nothing about a pattern.
questions.check: Did the agent open the account's own timeline/other posts, rather than relying on the follower count alone?
questions.say_example: A follower count alone shows no pattern. I'm opening the account's other posts to look.

questions.question: What channel, view count and timestamp does the debunking video show?
questions.why: Examining the channel name, low view count, and on-screen webcam timestamps helps determine the credibility of the debunking evidence.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to independently judge the reliability and bias of the secondary source used to disprove the claim.
questions.check: What are the channel name, subscriber or view count, and any on-screen timestamp shown on the video used to debunk the original claim?
questions.say_example: The debunking video comes from <a small channel, under 500 views>. Its timestamp says <2019>.

questions.question: What time, date and place does the image's overlay claim?
questions.why: Capturing the specific time, date, and coordinates shown in the red text is necessary to accurately verify the astronomical conditions for that exact moment and location.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the firsthand awareness of the exact timestamp and location details needed to independently evaluate the fact-check.
questions.check: What time, date, and coordinates does the on-screen overlay claim for the photo?
questions.say_example: Read the overlay's claim - <11:40 p.m., 3 March 2021>, near <a coastal town>

questions.question: Were the video's upload date and channel read before the claim was checked?
questions.why: Noting the upload date, channel name, and playing the video is necessary to establish exactly what claim needs to be verified.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally assess the initial tone and context of the source video before the investigation begins.
questions.verify_form: The agent may not have read the source video's upload date and channel before checking - check that it did; the claim's origin rests on those two.
questions.check: Did the agent note the video's upload date and channel name before checking the claim itself?
questions.say_example: The claim's origin rests on this video's upload date and channel. Neither was read yet.

questions.question: Do the messages contradict the city or name shown on the profile?
questions.why: The screen shows the sender making disjointed statements about being in Miami and Los Angeles, and introducing themselves despite their name already being in the chat header.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the intuitive human ability to read between the lines and detect unnatural conversational behavior that flags a fake persona.
questions.check: Do the chat messages contradict a detail already shown elsewhere on the page, such as the profile's or header's stated city or name?
questions.say_example: The chat says <Denver>. The profile lists <Tampa>. Same person, two cities.

questions.question: Was the photo itself reverse-searched, or only a description of it typed in?
questions.why: The presenter highlighted generic features in the photo like palm trees, mountains, and a fire, demonstrating that these details alone would produce search results that are too broad.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human intuition required to visually assess an image's geographical clues and determine whether a text search or a reverse image search is the better strategy.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose between a text search on what the photo shows and a reverse image search - check which it ran; loose details give loose results.
questions.check: Which method did the agent use to search - a plain text query describing the image's visible details, or a reverse image search on the photo itself?
questions.say_example: Details like <palm trees and mountains> are too generic for a text search. I'm running a reverse image search on the photo instead.

questions.question: Does the way the moon sits in the photo fit the place the claim says it was taken?
questions.why: Locating the Tycho crater at the bottom of the moon establishes its orientation, which proves the photo could not have been taken from the southern hemisphere as claimed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to apply your own geographic and astronomical knowledge to independently spot visual inconsistencies in the image.
questions.check: Where does the identifying feature, such as a crater, sit in the photo, and does that orientation fit the location the claim states?
questions.say_example: The crater sits at the bottom of the moon in this photo. That view only happens from the northern hemisphere, and the claim says <a southern city>.

questions.question: Were all of the profile's photos saved, or only the first?
questions.why: The profile page displayed another photo of the woman in sunglasses, which could provide a better match for a reverse-image search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the intuitive judgment to proactively gather supplementary evidence that might be the key to definitively verifying the claim.
questions.verify_form: The agent captured some of the profile's photos - check whether it took all of them or stopped at the first; in the recording only the third one matched.
questions.check: Did the agent capture all of the profile's photos, or stop after the first one?
questions.say_example: Only <1 of 3> profile photos was saved. The other <2> might be the ones that match.

questions.question: Does the search use the claim's own words, or a paraphrase?
questions.why: Typing a clear natural language question in the search box, as shown by the autocomplete suggestions for 'Where was Obama born?', sets the foundation for finding relevant fact-checks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide exactly which specific claim or urban legend they want to prioritize and investigate.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose one phrase or question to search - check it is the claim's own wording and not a paraphrase; the first phrase tried can find nothing.
questions.check: Does the search that ran use the claim's own exact wording, or a paraphrase of it?
questions.say_example: The search used <a paraphrase> instead of the claim's own words. Re-running it with the exact wording.

questions.question: Is the image taken from the Images tab the one in the post, or a similar photo?
questions.why: The default search results show text articles about the rumor, but clicking the Images tab is necessary to locate the exact visual material needed for the verification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually scan the search results and select the exact viral image you want to investigate.
questions.verify_form: The agent took the image from a text search's Images tab - check the image it took is the one that spread, not a similar photo of the same person.
questions.check: Is the image taken from the Images tab the one actually attached to the post, or a different photo of the same subject?
questions.say_example: The Images tab shows several photos of <the same person>. The one taken isn't the one in the post.

questions.question: Is the second search phrase from the email's body, or the headline again?
questions.why: Selecting a highly specific string of text from the email body increases the chances of finding an exact match in fact-checking databases if previous queries failed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to intuitively select the most distinct and searchable phrasing from the raw text based on your own reading comprehension.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a second phrase from the email after the first found nothing - check it is a sentence from the body and not the headline again.
questions.check: Is the next search phrase a sentence from the email's body, distinct from the headline already tried?
questions.say_example: The second try used the headline again. A sentence from the body would find more.

questions.question: Which line of the profile's text was searched for copies?
questions.why: Searching for the exact demographic and preference text shown on the profile helps identify if scammers are reusing the same bio across multiple fake accounts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to intuitively select which specific profile details are most likely to expose a copy-pasted scam account.
questions.verify_form: The agent searched some of the profile's text for cloned accounts - check which lines it used; the boilerplate sentences are the ones scammers reuse.
questions.check: Which line of the profile's text did the search use - a boilerplate self-description line, or something else?
questions.say_example: I searched <the profile's stock bio line> for copies. That's the line scammers reuse across fake accounts.

questions.question: Was the profile's photo saved, not only its text?
questions.why: The profile displays text details like a handle and location alongside a main photo, offering different starting points for verification.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to prioritize tracing the profile picture or investigating the text-based details.
questions.verify_form: The agent captured the profile's photo or its text - check which; the photo is what a reverse search needs.
questions.check: Did the agent capture the profile's photo, not only its text, before starting the reverse search?
questions.say_example: The profile's <bio text> was captured, but not its photo. A reverse search needs the photo.

questions.question: Which image from the collage was searched, the most distinctive one or just the first?
questions.why: Choosing the image with the most distinct visual elements, such as the Pope and the cross, ensures the reverse image search yields the most accurate results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to apply human intuition to determine which specific visual details are most likely to uncover the true origin of the post.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked one photo of the collage to search - check it is the one with the most distinct content and not the first.
questions.check: Is the selected image from the collage the one with the most distinct, searchable content, or just the first one in the set?
questions.say_example: The <first> photo in the collage was searched. <The one with the banner> has more to search on.

children.label: Ask the fact-checkers
children.note: 2.1 opens a fact-checker directly in fU9D and F6MD. In the other keepers, the fact-check turns up inside the match list instead, which is 3.6. Then 2.2, and 2.3 when the search finds nothing, which F6MD does once. 2.4 picks a result. 2.5 to 2.8 read the ruling: the label, whether it rules on the claim's exact wording, the example and the origins, the date - fU9D reads all four. linG and VOgi read a fact-check last, after their own verdict, and that is 8.3.

questions.question: Is a cookie banner, popup or paywall covering the fact-check's text?
questions.why: News and fact-checking websites frequently use large overlays that block the content until dismissed, which a sighted user would immediately notice and close so the audience can read along.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent is actually displaying visible, accessible text for the live session rather than scraping hidden DOM elements behind an overlay.
questions.check: Is a cookie banner, newsletter popup, or paywall currently covering the fact-check article's text?
questions.say_example: A pop-up is covering the article. Closing it so I can read the ruling.

questions.question: Is the original post or email still open in a tab while you search?
questions.why: Keeping the Gmail tab open ensures you can easily reference the exact wording of the 'sales tax on homes' claim while you search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to organize your browser tabs to ensure the original source material remains immediately accessible.
questions.verify_form: The agent searched in the same tab or a new one - check the original email is still open, so its wording can be held against the ruling.
questions.check: Is the original post or email still open in another tab for comparison, or was it closed when the new search tab opened?
questions.say_example: The original email closed when the search tab opened. Reopening it to compare the wording.

questions.question: Which fact-checking site was opened?
questions.why: Typing a specific, trusted URL into the address bar ensures you bypass potentially biased search results and go straight to an established fact-checker.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means you lose the ability to decide which specific fact-checking organization's methodology and editorial standards you trust most for this particular topic.
questions.verify_form: The agent went to one fact-checking site - check it is one you trust for this kind of claim; it typed the address itself.
questions.check: Which fact-checking site did the agent navigate to?
questions.say_example: Opened <Snopes> to check this

questions.question: Which fact-checkers does this tool actually cover?
questions.why: Reviewing sections like 'What fact checks are included?' and 'How can I restrict results?' ensures you understand the tool's methodology and limitations.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally evaluate the transparency and inclusion criteria of the fact-checking platform being used.
questions.verify_form: The agent read or skipped the tool's About page - check whether it knows which fact-checkers the tool covers before it treats a missing result as no fact-check.
questions.check: Did the agent check what the fact-check tool actually covers before treating an empty result as 'no fact-check exists anywhere'?
questions.say_example: This tool only covers <a few fact-checking sites>. Finding nothing here doesn't mean nobody has checked it.

questions.question: Did the search run on what was typed, or on a dropdown suggestion that changed it?
questions.why: Ignoring the auto-populated suggestions ensures your search query remains exactly as you intended without being influenced by popular search trends.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their exact, unbiased search phrasing was used if the agent defaults to clicking a potentially skewed auto-suggestion.
questions.verify_form: The agent may have clicked a suggestion from the dropdown - check whether the query that ran is yours or the suggestion's.
questions.check: Did the search run on a dropdown/autocomplete suggestion that changed or narrowed the typed query, or on the exact text typed?
questions.say_example: The search ran on a dropdown suggestion, <'stadium baseball game'>, instead of the term typed.

questions.question: What was typed into the Fact Check Explorer search box?
questions.why: The screen shows the Fact Check Explorer search bar, which is the starting point for finding existing fact-checks on a specific claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to specify the exact keywords or claim to search for in the fact-checking database.
questions.check: What topic or person's name is entered in the Fact Check Explorer's search bar?
questions.say_example: Searched Fact Check Explorer for <the moon claim>

questions.question: Are the results limited to the fact-checker you asked for?
questions.why: Confirming the search successfully filtered for 'site:fullfact.org' ensures you are properly targeting a reliable source before refining the query for your specific claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the peace of mind that the agent is correctly using site-specific search operators to consult trusted fact-checking organizations.
questions.check: Do the search results actually come from the specific site requested (e.g. a site: filter), or are they unrestricted?
questions.say_example: The results aren't limited to <fullfact.org>. The site filter didn't take.

questions.question: Did clicking the publisher tag keep your search term, or drop it?
questions.why: Clicking the 'Full Fact' tag replaced the 'brexit' search with just 'site:fullfact.org', bringing up completely unrelated claims like a Roe v Wade protest.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses accurate verification of their specific claim if the agent fails to notice the search query was overwritten and starts investigating unrelated topics.
questions.check: Did clicking the publisher/topic tag keep the original search term, or did it replace it with just the site filter, dropping the topic?
questions.say_example: Clicking the <Full Fact> tag dropped <the search term>. Now it's all of their articles, not your claim.

questions.question: After no matches, was a different or broader phrase tried?
questions.why: The search results page explicitly stated that no matches were found for the exact phrase, meaning a broader or different query was needed to find relevant fact-checks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to successfully verify the claim if the agent simply gives up after a single overly specific search fails.
questions.check: After the search returned no matches, did the agent try a different or broader phrase?
questions.say_example: No matches for <the exact phrase>. Retried with <a broader term>.

questions.question: After the fact-checkers turned up nothing, did the search move on to the original sources?
questions.why: Established fact-checkers take time to publish, so a persistent lack of results for a trending rumor means you must recognize the claim is too new and switch to investigating the raw sources yourself.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the flexibility to switch verification strategies when relying on established databases fails for breaking rumors.
questions.verify_form: The fact-checker searches kept finding nothing - check whether the agent moved on to the sources themselves or stopped; a new claim may not be checked anywhere yet.
questions.check: After several fact-checker searches return nothing, does the agent switch from searching fact-checker databases to tracing the primary sources directly?
questions.say_example: Fact-checkers turned up nothing after <3> tries. Checking the original sources directly instead.

questions.question: Does a known fact-checker address this exact image?
questions.why: Finding the Alt News tweet with the 'fact-check' stamp and [address] movie details provides authoritative confirmation that the viral claim is false.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct reassurance of seeing a recognized fact-checker's visual stamp and specific contextual details debunking the claim.
questions.check: Does a recognized fact-checker's post or article address this specific image?
questions.say_example: Found a ruling on this exact image from <Snopes>

questions.question: Was a fact-checker's page opened, or a general news article or blog?
questions.why: The search results display both general news sites like Time and dedicated fact-checkers like Snopes, making it important to prioritize the specialized fact-checking source.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your personal trust preferences and media literacy when selecting which specific fact-checking organization to rely on.
questions.verify_form: The agent opened one of the results - check it is a fact-checker's page and not a news outlet's or a blog's; the results listed both.
questions.check: Did the agent open a dedicated fact-checker's page, or a general news/blog article instead?
questions.say_example: Opened <a general news article> instead of <the fact-checker's own page> listed below it.

questions.question: Were the other results looked at, or only the first one opened?
questions.why: The screen shows you immediately clicking the top search result, which skips the crucial step of scanning multiple sources to find the most authoritative context.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the verification is based on a thorough lateral reading of multiple independent sources rather than just the most search-engine-optimized result.
questions.verify_form: The agent opened the first result - check whether it scanned the others; the first is the search engine's pick, not the best match.
questions.check: Did the agent look at more than one search result before opening one, or open only the first result listed?
questions.say_example: The first result was opened right away. <A fact-checker's page> further down wasn't looked at.

questions.question: Was the full fact-check opened, or only the cut-off snippet read?
questions.why: The search result summary cuts off mid-sentence, meaning the full explanation of the rating is hidden unless the article is opened.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the detailed evidence and context behind the fact-checker's verdict.
questions.verify_form: The agent read the rating off the results snippet or opened the article - check which; the snippet cuts the explanation mid-sentence.
questions.check: Did the agent open the full fact-check article, or rely on the search result's truncated snippet?
questions.say_example: Only the search snippet was read, and it cuts off mid-sentence. Opening the full article.

questions.question: What rating does the meter or graphic on the fact-checker's page show?
questions.why: Sites like PolitiFact use a visual 'Truth-O-Meter' graphic (e.g., 'Pants on Fire') that conveys the definitive verdict at a glance, which might lack descriptive alt-text for screen readers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate, definitive verdict conveyed by the visual rating graphic if the agent only reads the surrounding article text.
questions.check: Does the fact-checker's page show its rating through a graphic or meter (e.g. a dial or icon) with a label, and what does that label say?
questions.say_example: The rating is shown as a meter graphic. It reads <Pants on Fire>.

questions.question: What is the fact-checker's verdict on the claim?
questions.why: The Snopes article displays a 'MIXTURE OF TRUE AND FALSE INFORMATION' rating, breaking down exactly which parts of the real estate tax rumor are accurate.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the nuanced understanding of which specific details in the viral claim are true versus false.
questions.check: What rating or verdict label does the fact-checker's page give (e.g. True, False, Mixture)?
questions.say_example: The fact-checker rates this <Mixture of True and False>.

questions.question: Is this fact-check about your claim, or a different one that uses the same photo?
questions.why: The Yahoo Finance headline addresses a rumor about a 'Muslim leader' and a 'dalit woman,' while the original tweet claimed the image showed violence against Hindus in Bengal, revealing that this same movie still is repeatedly recycled for different sectarian rumors.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the broader context of how this specific piece of media is weaponized across multiple different misinformation campaigns.
questions.check: Does the fact-check's body, not just its headline, rule on the same claim the post makes?
questions.say_example: This fact-check covers <a different rumor using the same photo>. It isn't a ruling on the claim in your post.

questions.question: What exact wording does the fact-checker quote as the claim it checked?
questions.why: Seeing the exact 'CAN OBAMA BE PRESIDENT?' text in the example box establishes the precise claim before evaluating the fact-checker's detailed explanation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to read the original wording of the viral claim, which provides crucial context for understanding the fact-checker's subsequent breakdown.
questions.check: What is the exact rumor text quoted in the fact-checker's Example box?
questions.say_example: Read the ruling's example box - it quotes <'the tax applies to every home sale'>

questions.question: Is the basis of the ruling stated near the top of the Origins section?
questions.why: The screen shows a lengthy 'Origins' section detailing the law, forcing a choice between gathering complete context and saving time.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide that the specific details of the legislation are personally irrelevant and can be skipped.
questions.verify_form: The agent read the full origins section or skimmed it - check which; the part that matters is the basis of the tax, near the top.
questions.check: Is the key basis of the ruling (e.g. what a tax actually applies to) stated near the top of the Origins/legislation section, or buried further down?
questions.say_example: The first lines of Origins give the basis of the ruling, <a tax on gains over a threshold>. I skipped the rest.

questions.question: When was this fact-check last updated?
questions.why: Checking the 'Last updated: 17 October 2008' timestamp at the bottom of the page reveals whether the research might be missing recent developments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the intuitive sense of how outdated the evidence might be when evaluating the overall reliability of the verdict.
questions.check: What last-updated date does the fact-check page show, and is it years old or earlier than the post being checked?
questions.say_example: This fact-check was last updated <March 2017>. That's well before the post you sent, so it may not cover this version.

children.label: Run the reverse image search
children.note: 3.1 picks the engine - most keepers go straight to Google without considering another engine, qW96 and linG weigh Yandex, ZEyc takes TinEye. then 3.2, where the user puts the image in by one of five routes. 3.3 is where the engine offers a crop. 3.4 and 3.5 happen on every results page. 3.6 picks the match to open. 3.7 runs the search again with a clearer copy, another engine or another route - 6KeC, qW96, lCH7, p5e9, ZEyc and N2gv all run more than one search. 3.8 in qW96 alone. 3.9 does not appear in any of the recordings.

questions.question: If the original post or report is gone or paywalled, was an archived copy opened instead?
questions.why: Misinformers often delete their posts when debunked, so retrieving the archived version is necessary to prove the claim was actually made and see its original context.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the investigative persistence to use web archives when live links fail, which can prematurely halt an investigation.
questions.verify_form: The source link was dead and the agent stopped or looked for an archived copy - check which; the archive is where a deleted post survives.
questions.check: If the original post or the key report is deleted, dead or paywalled, did the agent open an archived or syndicated copy instead of stopping?
questions.say_example: The original post is gone. Checking the <Wayback Machine> copy instead of stopping there.

questions.question: Which reverse image engine was used, and does it show first-found dates?
questions.why: The screen lists multiple reverse image search options like Google, TinEye, and Pixsy, so you must select one to proceed with tracing the image's origin.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over which specific reverse image search engine is used to investigate the visual evidence.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked one engine from the list - check which; only some report a first-found date.
questions.check: Which reverse image engine did the agent choose, and does that engine report a first-found/upload date for matches?
